questions.text: I schedule regular maintenance for my car, home, and other possessions.
I tend to accept praise graciously and use it as fuel for further personal achievement.
I would take on a second job to support a family member's dream.
I find that spending an afternoon helping a friend move is more rewarding than spending it on my own pursuits.
I do not usually notice when someone is nervous during a conversation unless they say so.
I find it hard to detect when someone is being supportive on the surface but competitive underneath.
I notice when an email is bcc'd to someone based on the overly formal tone.
I routinely turn down invitations that do not serve my personal interests or growth.
When I recognize that someone could be seriously hurt, preventing that harm matters to me personally.
When someone is suffering, its claim on me is immediate; I don't need a further reason.
When I connect deeply with someone, the intensity of that bond registers as a physical sensation.
I prefer to set the ground rules before any group activity begins.
I can feel the residue of a stressful phone call still buzzing in my body an hour later.
I can sense when two people are pretending to get along but actually dislike each other.
When I hear about a group of people in serious trouble, I seldom feel any concern for them.
I resist starting new projects until current ones are at a natural stopping point.
I experience the ebb and flow of life at a volume that never requires me to adjust.
I tend to re-feel past emotional experiences at nearly their original intensity when I remember them.
Someone's tears or visible distress rarely change what I want to do.
When I hear that someone is having a hard time, I usually wish things would go better for them.
I do not naturally decode the layers of meaning in polite conversation.
I naturally position myself at the center of decision-making networks.
I always consult with my team before making commitments that involve them.
When I have a vision, I wait to see if others share it before moving forward.
I give my full attention to what's happening now and prepare for future obligations closer to the time.
I find that saying no to requests that dilute my focus is one of my most valuable habits.
I feel a responsibility to contribute more than my fair share.
I prefer to let my day unfold naturally rather than follow a rigid schedule.
I tend to wait and see if the group will name the elephant in the room on its own.
I can tell when two people in a room are aware of each other even when they are not interacting.
I approach important decisions by gathering information and analyzing options systematically.
I rarely make backup plans because I trust my ability to improvise if things go sideways.
I notice that excitement in me feels like a pleasant warmth rather than a roaring fire.
I find it hard to stay quiet when I disagree with the group's direction.
I can be in the middle of a crisis and still feel internally composed.
Learning about serious harm to people far away leaves me with little wish to see it end.
